prize_parts.citation: For the development of targeted protein degradation, harnessing the ubiquitin-proteasome system through PROTACs and molecular glue degraders

statement.case_for: Targeted protein degradation is a new chemical principle, event-driven and catalytic induced proximity, rather than an incremental improvement. It rests on a mechanistic base that has been confirmed by many independent laboratories: ternary-complex formation, E3 ligase recruitment, and cereblon as the molecular target that explains thalidomide-class glues. It is the one shortlisted candidate that a clear majority of us placed in the top three (seven of eight members). Crews and Deshaies founded the PROTAC concept and Handa's identification of cereblon supplies the glue strand, so this trio covers both halves of the ballot title. I still regard Gray and Winkler's work on long-range protein electron transfer (B056) as the cleanest mechanistic science on the list, and I ranked it first. But I have to be honest that it has no support beyond my own ballot, and my enthusiasm comes partly from my own field of biological energy conversion. A prize configuration needs to survive discussion, and B029 is the one that can.
statement.case_against: No PROTAC has yet been approved as a drug, so clinical vindication is incomplete. The credit is contested: Ciulli's VHL ligands and structural work made the approach rational, Sakamoto, Gray, Ito and Kim all have claims, and the PROTAC and glue lineages are historically distinct, so a three-name limit will exclude people many would call essential. If the committee considers the discovery too early or too tangled in credit, the stable alternative is a scientifically cleaner, older achievement such as B056.

responses.point: Aili ranked B029 first, with Crews, Deshaies and Handa, arguing that the concept is a new pharmacological modality with a solid mechanistic foundation despite pending approvals.
responses.response: I agree on the science and have moved to your trio, replacing the Ciulli name I used in my opening. Handa gives the molecular glue strand a principled place in the prize. I would resist treating the absence of an approved degrader as minor, though. It leaves the claim of impact resting on the mechanism and on trial pipelines, so the citation should emphasise the chemical concept rather than therapeutic outcomes.

responses.point: Linke, as chair, ranked halide perovskites (B058) first for original chemistry and physics of defect-tolerant absorbers, while acknowledging stability and scale-up are unresolved.
responses.response: I take the point that the efficiency rise is real and widely reproduced. My reservation is that the open problems of stability, lead content and scale-up concern whether the technology works, and the physical mechanism of defect tolerance is still being worked out. The credit is also split among at least six claimants, and the three-name cut (Miyasaka, Park, Snaith) leaves out Grätzel, Seok and Kanatzidis. I think B058 is further from a stable, assignable discovery than B029 is, and I would like to hear how you would handle Kojima and Grätzel.

responses.point: Zou ranked base editing (B047) first with Liu, Komor and Gaudelli, calling it an original chemical invention that is already clinical, with timing that is right.
responses.response: I find the chemistry convincing, and I rated it fourth. My concern is the 2020 CRISPR prize, which makes a second genome-editing prize delicate, and prime editing, which sits in a separate ballot. If we reward base editing, I would want the committee to decide whether Liu alone or Liu with two former trainees is right before we settle. Kondo and Nishida's independent deaminase fusion also weakens an exclusive claim. I rank it a credible alternative rather than the lead.

responses.point: Åqvist ranked Car-Parrinello molecular dynamics (B027) first as a foundational method with a clean two-person attribution and an overdue recognition.
responses.response: The attribution is indeed the cleanest on the list, and ab initio dynamics of proton transfer in condensed phases touches my own interests. The difficulty is that computational chemistry was recognised in 1998 and 2013, and the committee may feel that area is already served. I also note that your ballot is the only one that ranks it first, so I would like to know whether you see it as stronger than B029 on scientific merit alone, rather than on attribution tidiness.

responses.point: Sparr ranked biomolecular phase separation (B055) first as a physical-chemistry concept with more than a decade of confirmation, while noting the credit is crowded.
responses.response: I share your sense that it is conceptually generative, and the physical-chemistry framing is attractive. But the central question of which cellular assemblies are functionally driven by phase separation is still contested, and Pappu and Mittag would be excluded by a three-person cut. I think it is less mature than the degradation work, where the underlying mechanism is not in doubt.

uncertainties: Whether Crews, Deshaies and Handa is the right trio, or whether Ciulli should replace one of them, given his VHL-ligand and ternary-complex structural work.
Whether PROTACs and molecular glues are one achievement or two, and whether a compound citation can be made coherent within three names.
Whether the absence of an approved degrader drug should lead the committee to wait.
Whether B056 (Gray and Winkler) can attract support beyond my own ballot, given the 1992 Marcus prize.
statement.conflict_note: No formal conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I note that my own research on respiratory-chain electron and proton transfer is close to B056, which could bias my enthusiasm for B056, and that I am a Stockholm University colleague of Xiaodong Zou, though she is not a candidate.
